# The Cairngorms National Park

Scroll down


## The Cairngorms is simply inspiring!

It has something for everyone, from exploring nature and wildlife in the mountains, to adventures in ancient woodlands or taking a dip in one of our freshwater Lochs.

The Cairngorms National Park has spectacular landscapes from wild, high mountains, to heather moorlands, magnificent forests, lowland farms and crofts, wetlands and rivers which wind through the flood plains – as the biggest and most northerly National Park in Britain, it is simply awe-inspiring.

## Key activities

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/CB-Big-Weekend-17-117-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Walking , Activity

Set in spectacular scenery there are short low-level walks, longer hikes through woodlands and mountains,  multi-day long distance walks and mountain top routes to choose from, where ever you are in the Park.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Europarc2018-1-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Wildlife watching , Activity

Come to the Cairngorms to see Scotland’s rare and iconic wildlife for yourself.  Keep your eyes peeled for darting red squirrels and soaring ospreys, go out with a guide or watch from a hide – the choice is yours!

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/visitscotland_39122291628-mr-600x400.jpg)

Activity

### Outdoor Activities , Activity

The Park offers something for everyone – water sports, snow sports, incredible walking and cycling routes, plus 12 golf courses. It even has the first permanent bridge-based bungee jump in the UK.

![Special qualities](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/visitscotland_38724035412-lr-1840x1080.jpg)

## Special qualities

10 reasons why the Cairngorms is a special place

Adventure – Cycling and biking is one of the many ways to explore and discover the sights, nature and wildlife in the Park. All types of cycling are catered for from family-friendly routes, stunning rides on quiet roads to some of the best mountain bike trails in Scotland for all ages and abilities.

Castles & Gatherings – Explore the past by visiting our castles and historical sites, immerse yourself in the culture of the Cairngorms through our local music, ceilidhs and highland games.

Dark Skies – The Tomintoul and Glenlivet area is one of the best places to see a night sky brimming with stars. Some brilliant vantage points and vast horizons have seen the area awarded the prestigious status of International Dark Sky Park and is the most Northerly Dark Sky Park in the world and among the darkest skies in the UK!

Family Fun – The Cairngorms National Park is a world-renowned area where both residents and visitors, especially families, can enjoy an unparalleled range of outdoor recreation opportunities with something for everyone no matter what age, ability or interest.

Food & Drink – Few regions in Scotland encapsulate the traditional and world-famous cuisine of the country as well as the Cairngorms – venison from deer that range across the hills, beef from Highland cattle and hardy rare breeds, salmon and trout from pristine rivers and lochs and whisky from age-old distilleries.

Hospitality – Providing a warm welcome and exceptional experiences to people from near and far is part of our culture in the Cairngorms National Park.  Voted one of the top destinations in the world, visitors ‘love this place’.

Landscapes – The Cairngorms National Park is hugely diverse; it is a living, working landscape from the wild high mountains, to the heather moorlands and peatlands, to the magnificent forests, the farms and crofts, and the wetlands and rivers which wind through the flood plains.

Scenic Routes – Whether travelling by bike, car or on foot, there are plenty of places to stop and take in the natural beauty of the landscape.

Stories & Culture – Separated by the great bulk of the mountains, different areas of the Park have their own distinct identity and cultural traditions, but they share deep connections to the same environments. Explore Scotland’s Gaelic language through our place names and unique stories that they tell of the Park.

Wildlife – The wildlife in the National Park is outstanding. It is a stronghold for many rare and endangered species, living in some of our most natural landscapes.

## Did you know?

The Cairngorms are the largest, most northerly National Park in the UK and has the highest range of mountains - sitting high above sea level you would be forgiven for thinking you were in the Arctic on some of the highest plateaux in the world. It is home to some of the most iconic wildlife species, some living high up on the mountain tops of the Park.

# Wild and Wonderful

The Cairngorms is celebrated as a place of wildness. The feeling of being surrounded by wildlife and natural habitats helps us reconnect with nature, and refreshes the mind and body.  It is hard to describe the outstanding nature and landscapes of the Cairngorms National Park, its importance for the people who live and work here, the people who visit and enjoy the area and the significance of the wildlife and habitats supported by this special place.  This is a place hugely valued by many people as well as wildlife. The Cairngorms is home to a quarter of the UK’s rare and endangered species. It contains Scotland’s largest, most natural habitats and is where the country’s most ambitious, landscape-scale conservation action is taking place.  It is home to 18,500 residents and welcomes over 2 million visitors each year.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/visitscotland_38724035412-lr-1840x1080.jpg)

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Picture-015-lr-580x580.jpg)

### Plan your visit

Whether you are looking for adventure, fun for the whole family or a break from the everyday– the Cairngorms National Park has a lot to offer so let us help you [plan your visit](https://cairngorms.co.uk/discover-explore/enjoying-the-park/planning-a-visit/).Situated in the heart of the Scottish Highlands, the National Park is easy to reach by road, rail, plane or bike. We have direct train links to Inverness, Glasgow, Edinburgh and London.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/Festival-for-All-035-580x580.jpg)

### Travelling on a budget

There are many [things to see and do in the Park that won’t break the bank](https://cairngorms.co.uk/discover-explore/planning-a-visit/on-a-shoestring/) and some that are completely free.

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/170627AboyneAwayDayFinzeanForEmail-Cairngorms-580x580.jpg)

### A park for all

If you or a family member have accessibility requirements, there are plenty of easy-access paths to enjoy, accessible activities and attractions to visit as well as accessible facilities and services available to you. For more information visit [Access for All](https://cairngorms.co.uk/discover-explore/planning-a-visit/access4all/) in the Cairngorms National Park. We look forward to welcoming you to our special place!

Whether you are looking for a solo escape, fun for the whole family or just a break from the everyday, the Cairngorms National Park has it all.

Situated right in the heart of the Scottish highlands, the UK’s largest National Park has a spectacular combination of wilderness, heritage, adventure and peace. This National Park is known and revered for its natural and environmental credentials, and so it makes sense that the love of this place must go hand in hand with action to protect and take care of the nature and wildlife that depends on it.

The Cairngorms welcomes around 2 million people a year, so the positive impact that visitors can have should not be underestimated. From small actions like litter picking, packing reusable picnic tubs and shopping locally, to cutting the carbon and taking the train, planning ahead provides the opportunity to put sustainability at the core of your trip, ensuring that future generations can benefit from all the National Park has to offer for many years to come.

Like all other [national parks in the UK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_the_UK "National parks of the UK"), the park is [IUCN designated Category V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_protected_area_categories "IUCN protected area categories"). However, it contains within its boundaries several [national nature reserves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_nature_reserve_(Scotland) "National nature reserve (Scotland)") that have IUCN Category II (national park) statuses, such as [Abernethy Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abernethy_Forest "Abernethy Forest") and [Mar Lodge Estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar_Lodge_Estate "Mar Lodge Estate").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-keyfacts-4) In 2018, 1.9 million tourism visits were recorded.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-Sustainable_Tourism-5) The majority of visitors are domestic, with 25 per cent coming from elsewhere in the UK, and 21 per cent being from other countries.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-f&f-6) Tourism makes up about 80% of the economy of the national park.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-keyfacts-4) [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Sign_at_Cairngorm_Mountain_Railway_base.jpg/250px-Sign_at_Cairngorm_Mountain_Railway_base.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sign_at_Cairngorm_Mountain_Railway_base.jpg) Sign at Cairngorm Mountain Railway base ## Geography \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cairngorms_National_Park&action=edit§ion=1 "Edit section: Geography")\] [![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f7/Drumochter_Pass_-_geograph.org.uk_-_333811.jpg/250px-Drumochter_Pass_-_geograph.org.uk_-_333811.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Drumochter_Pass_-_geograph.org.uk_-_333811.jpg) The Pass of Drumochter is the main route into the national park from the south. The Cairngorms National Park covers an area of 4,528km2 (1,748sqmi) in the [council areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdivisions_of_Scotland "Subdivisions of Scotland") of [Aberdeenshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeenshire "Aberdeenshire"), [Moray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moray "Moray"), [Highland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland_(council_area) "Highland (council area)"), [Angus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus,_Scotland "Angus, Scotland") and [Perth and Kinross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth_and_Kinross "Perth and Kinross").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-sitelink-1) The mountain range of the Cairngorms lies at the heart of the national park, but forms only one part of it, alongside other hill ranges such as the [Angus Glens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_Glens "Angus Glens") and the [Monadhliath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monadhliath "Monadhliath"), and lower areas like [Strathspey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strathspey,_Scotland "Strathspey, Scotland") and upper [Deeside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Dee,_Aberdeenshire "River Dee, Aberdeenshire").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-cnp-landscape-7) Three major rivers rise in the park: the [Spey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Spey "River Spey"), the [Dee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Dee_(Aberdeenshire) "River Dee (Aberdeenshire)"), and the [Don](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Don,_Aberdeenshire "River Don, Aberdeenshire"). The Spey, which is the second longest river in Scotland, rises in the Monadhliath, whilst the Dee and the Don both rise in the Cairngorms themselves.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-f&f-6) The Cairngorms themselves are a spectacular landscape, similar in appearance to the [Hardangervidda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardangervidda "Hardangervidda") National Park of Norway in having a large area of upland plateau.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] The range consists of three main plateaux at about 1000–1200m above sea level, above which domed summits (the eroded stumps of once much higher mountains)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAllenDavidson2012Prologue:_The_Mountains,_p._1/14-8) rise to around 1300m. Many of the summits have [tors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tor_(rock_formation) "Tor (rock formation)"), free-standing rock outcrops that stand on top of the boulder-strewn landscape.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-cnp-Landscape-9) The edges of the plateaux are in places steep cliffs of granite and they are excellent for [skiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiing "Skiing"), [rock climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_climbing "Rock climbing") and [ice climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_climbing "Ice climbing"). The Cairngorms form an [arctic-alpine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic-alpine "Arctic-alpine") mountain environment, with [tundra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tundra "Tundra")-like characteristics and long-lasting snow patches.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-cnp-Landscape-9) The [Monadhliath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monadhliath "Monadhliath") mountains lie to the north of Strathspey, and comprise a bleak, wide plateau rising to between 700 and 950m.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-sheet35-10)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-11) Two major transport routes run through the park, with both the [A9 road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A9_road_(Scotland) "A9 road (Scotland)") and the [Highland Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland_Main_Line "Highland Main Line") crossing over the [Pass of Drumochter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pass_of_Drumochter "Pass of Drumochter") and running along Strathspey, providing links between the western and northern parts of the park and the cities of [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth,_Scotland "Perth, Scotland") and [Inverness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverness "Inverness"). The Highland Main Line is the only mainline rail route through the park, however there are several other major roads, including the [A86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A86_road "A86 road"), which links Strathspey to [Fort William](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_William,_Highland "Fort William, Highland"), and the [A93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A93_road "A93 road"), which links the Deeside area of the park to both Perth and [Aberdeen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdeen "Aberdeen").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-sheet42-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-sheet43-13)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-sheet35-10) ## Geology \[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cairngorms_National_Park&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Geology")\] Main article: [Geology of the Cairngorms National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geology_of_the_Cairngorms_National_Park "Geology of the Cairngorms National Park") The majority of the rocks within the Cairngorms National Park belong to the [Dalradian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalradian "Dalradian") [Supergroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stratigraphic_unit#Supergroup "Stratigraphic unit"), a thick sequence of sands, muds and [limestones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone "Limestone") that were deposited between about 800 and 600 million years ago on the margins of the former continent of [Laurentia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurentia "Laurentia").[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-14) Rocks now ascribed to the [Moine Supergroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moine_Supergroup "Moine Supergroup") occur along the northwestern edge of the Park. These Dalradian and Moine successions were intensely [faulted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fault_(geology) "Fault (geology)"), folded and [metamorphosed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphism "Metamorphism") during the [Caledonian Orogeny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caledonian_Orogeny "Caledonian Orogeny") between about 490 and 430 million years ago.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-p18-15) Geologists recognize a 'Grampian event', centred around 470 million years ago, which was responsible for the initial deformation of the Dalradian and relates to the collision of a [volcanic island arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volcanic_arc "Volcanic arc") with Laurentia over a period of about 20 million years. The subsequent collision of [Baltica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltica "Baltica") with Laurentia caused the 'Scandian event' which involved further folding and faulting of the Dalradian rock sequence. The [Great Glen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Glen_Fault "Great Glen Fault"), Ericht-Laidon and Glen Tilt faults were all active as [strike-slip faults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike-slip_fault "Strike-slip fault") at this time and may have played a part in allowing large [plutons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pluton "Pluton") of [granite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granite "Granite") to rise up amongst the Dalradian rocks and then cool in situ.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-16) The largest of these plutons is the granite mass which forms the Cairngorms themselves and which was emplaced around 427 million years ago. It is thought that the pluton had been unroofed within 20 million years of its emplacement and that the present landscape of the Cairngorms had begun to form by 390 million years ago. Evidence suggests that the granite currently at the surface was initially to be found at a depth of between 4 and 7km.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park#cite_note-p18-15) Other than a small [outlier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inliers_and_outliers_(geology) "Inliers and outliers (geology)") of [Old Red Sandstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Red_Sandstone "Old Red Sandstone"), there are no younger solid rocks within the national park. [Visiting](https://cairngorms.co.uk/visiting)

The Cairngorms is a spectacular place to visit, live and work, and by taking care of it we can all help to look after this special place for years to come.

The National Park welcomes around 2 million visitors every year, but it’s also a living, working landscape that is home to vibrant communities and rare wildlife. By planning ahead visitors can have a positive impact on the area, minimising their impact on the environment and making the most of their adventure.

Access rights in Scotland differ from the rest of the UK, so the first thing to do is become familiar with the [Scottish Outdoor Access Code](https://www.outdooraccess-scotland.scot/) before you arrive in the National Park.

The code gives more information on how you can help take care of the great outdoors, and has three key principles:

- Respect the interests of others
- Care for the environment
- Take responsibility for your own actions

While discovering the beauty of the Cairngorms, visitors may come across more unfamiliar or challenging locations, such as working farms, estates and areas protected for their conservation value. Learning more about how to approach these situations means respecting the people and nature of the National Park and preserving these landscapes for current and future generations to enjoy.

Here you’ll find some of the answers to our most commonly asked questions!

Do I have the right to roam?


You have the right to responsible access, which gives you a huge amount of freedom to explore most of the land and inland water of this special place, as long as you act responsibly in line with the Scottish Outdoor Access Code and you “leave no trace”.

This means you have the right of access for recreational (non-motorised) activities (like walking, cycling, horse riding, swimming and paddle sports) which you can do across most land and inland water.

There are some places where access rights don’t apply such as private gardens, farmyards and sports pitches when play is in progress. Wherever you are, you must always follow any reasonable advice or diversions eg when land management operations are taking place.

The Cairngorms is a unique and special place that people have explored for centuries. We welcome people to continue to enjoy the National Park while following the Scottish Outdoor Access Code, which has three key principles:

- Respect the interests of others.
- Care for the environment.
- Take responsibility for your own actions.

If we continue to do this, together we can preserve the nature and landscapes of the Cairngorms National Park for future generations to enjoy.

Check out our [‘need to know’ pages](https://cairngorms.co.uk/visiting/need-to-know) for more information on how to do this.

Can I light a fire?


Please do not light a fire in the National Park. We recommend using a gas stove for cooking. Open fires can be a cause of wildfires, which can be devastating for communities, wildlife and nature in the National Park.

At times of ‘high fire risk’ do not light any fire or BBQ in the National Park, always ensure cigarettes are fully extinguished and take your litter (including glass) away with you. It only takes one spark to cause devastation.

[Find everything you need to know on campfires and barbeques here.](https://cairngorms.co.uk/visiting/need-to-know/campfires-and-barbecues)

Where can I park my campervan?


The best thing to do is use a campsite or a designated overnight parking area, there are a number of great campsites nestled amongst the valleys and forests of the National Park that have all the facilities you might need, and great local places to eat and drink nearby.

[Plan your visit in your caravan or campervan, and find overnight options here.](https://cairngorms.co.uk/visiting/plan-your-visit/camping-and-campervans)

Where are the toilets?


There are a whole host of public toilets in the villages and towns of the National Park, but if you’re thinking of going more remote, then you will need to learn what to do when you need to “go” in the outdoors!

You might think, what’s the harm? You’re just one person! But what happens if everyone thinks that? Don’t risk someone stepping in your waste, or a local ranger having to clear it up. Unless you follow best practice, you could be polluting water courses and causing harm to wildlife.

The best thing to do is plan ahead and carry a toilet kit (trowel, plastic bags, toilet paper and hand sanitiser). If you need to go to the toilet, go at least 30 metres from lochs, rivers and streams and if you need to poo dig a hole and bury it, and replace the turf. Bag up and take any toilet paper and sanitary items away with you. Job done.

[Mountaineering Scotland have more great advice.](https://www.mountaineering.scot/safety-and-skills/health-and-hygiene/outdoor-toileting)

Can I fly a drone?


Recreational and personal use of drones is not directly covered by access rights and local restrictions may apply. You should check with the landowner or occupier for permission to use a drone.

More generally the use of drones is regulated by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) and their regulations around licensing are a legal requirement for flying any drone. Please note - new legal requirements came into force on 1 January 2026 and most drone operators are now required to register with the CAA and pass a theory test to gain a Flyer ID.

The [CAA Drone Code](https://www.caa.co.uk/drones/getting-started-with-drones-and-model-aircraft/drone-code/drone-code-overview/) must be adhered to, with an emphasis placed on personal responsibility. This includes:

- Respecting other people, their safety and privacy – there are restrictions (depending on the size of drone) as to how close you can fly to a person, vehicle or building. You should also not fly over crowds.
- Not flying anywhere where you will disturb or endanger wildlife or animals (including livestock). Restrictions may also exist in areas specifically designated for wildlife such as Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI’s), or where protected species are nesting that you might disturb.

Can I use an electric scooter, segway or e-foil?


No, products like hoverboards, segways, electric scooters (go-peds), powered unicycles, trolling motors on boats, SUP motors and efoils etc. are classified as powered transport, and these types of electric transports cannot be used in the Cairngorms National Park in any area of countryside or on any public road.

These powered transports are not within access rights and can only be used on private land / water where you have the express permission of the landowner.

Electric bikes are classed as a type of pedal cycle and can be used in the countryside in the same way that a standard bicycle can. To meet this definition, e-bikes must have pedals to propel it, a limited speed of 15.5 miles per hour, a maximum power output of 250 watts and a plate showing manufacturer and these details.

Am I allowed to collect mushrooms?


Yes, you can pick wild mushrooms and berries for your own consumption, but for your own safety, and to care for the environment, you should always follow the guidance in the [Scottish Wild Mushroom Code](https://cairngorms.co.uk/documents/the-scottish-wild-mushroom-code).

Please note that if you are collecting mushrooms for commercial purposes or for profit then legally you must have the permission of the landowner.

When does low ground shooting take place?


Pheasant shooting takes place during the autumn and winter in woods and forests and on adjacent open ground.  During this time, it is best to avoid game rearing pens and keep your dog on a lead or at heel when close to a pen.

Grouse shooting takes place on moorland areas, the season runs from 12 August to 10 December, with most shoots taking place during the early part of the season.

It’s helpful to be aware when shooting might be taking place and look for advice on alternative routes. Where possible, avoid crossing land where a shoot is taking place.

Do I need permission to run an event?


It might be necessary to seek landowner permission for an event that you are planning to run, especially if it’s a large or significant event.

We have a guidance document that has been written to help event organisers and land managers in the planning and management of organised outdoor events in the National Park. It may also provide helpful tips for many other people, including community groups, businesses and public agencies - anyone who is interested in outdoor events -and how they are managed.

[Download the outdoor access event guidance.](https://cairngorms.co.uk/documents/outdoor-access-events-guidance)

VisitCairngorms have also produced a helpful [Event Planners Guide](https://traveltrade.visitcairngorms.com/organising-an-event-in-the-cairngorms/) which will help you find locations and venues, plan transport links and connect with communities, suppliers and local businesses.

How do I prevent a tick bite?


The Cairngorms National Park is a great place for getting outdoors but like the rest of Scotland, you should protect yourself from the tiny biting parasites known as ticks.

Top tips for preventing a tick bite are:

- Stick to paths and avoid long grass, bracken, and heather.
- Cover exposed skin if you are walking through long grass, bracken, and heather.
- Use a recommended insect repellent.
- Most importantly check yourself for ticks at regular intervals, including in the days after getting outdoors.

For advice on removing ticks, the signs and symptoms of Lyme disease and when to see a doctor, visit this [NHS Inform page for guidance](https://www.nhsinform.scot/illnesses-and-conditions/injuries/skin-injuries/tick-bites).
